\title{The Benefit of Cross-Modal Fusion Is a Property of the Encoder,\\
Not of Its Capacity}

\author{Anonymous ACL submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Hateful meme detection requires combining an image with its text, and the
established architectures do so by multiplying two projected feature vectors
element-wise. That mechanism has been reported to give no advantage for a
language the encoder never saw, a failure attributed to misaligned feature
spaces; the attribution had not been tested. We test it. Four frozen encoders
are trained on the Hateful Memes Challenge over 15 seeds each, and
every encoder's cross-modal alignment is measured independently of training by
zero-shot retrieval on Crossmodal-3600. The fusion benefit changes sign with
the encoder, from +0.87 AUROC to $-$1.68, every cell significant
after correcting for multiplicity. The decisive control is a pair of encoders
from one family that differ by 3.42 AUROC in absolute score yet
whose fusion benefits are statistically \emph{equivalent} under a two
one-sided test against a pre-registered margin, so capacity is not what
decides. We then test the proposed explanation over 20 encoder-language
cells and it fails: alignment does not predict the fusion benefit
($r = -0.161$, $p = 0.499$), and neither dropping the cells near chance,
nor correcting for measurement error, nor fitting each language separately
recovers a relationship. What generalises is dependence on the encoder, not
the alignment axis. We release code, configurations and every per-seed record.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

A hateful meme carries its meaning across two modalities at once: an image
that is innocuous alone and a caption that is innocuous alone can be hateful
together. Architectures for this task therefore combine the two feature
vectors explicitly rather than classifying a concatenation of them. The
dominant mechanism is the element-wise product of a projected image vector and
a projected text vector --- the diagonal of their outer product, which
\citet{kumar2022hateclipper} call \emph{align} fusion.

That paper also reports a failure. On Tamil, its fusion variants gave no
advantage over plain concatenation, and the authors attribute this to
misaligned feature spaces for a language the encoder never saw. The
attribution is plausible, it is widely repeated, and as far as we can
establish it has never been tested. It names a cause without measuring it.

This paper measures it. We vary the encoder across four frozen models that
differ deliberately in language coverage, hold every architectural
hyperparameter fixed, and obtain each encoder's cross-modal alignment from a
source that no training touches. We then ask whether the first quantity
predicts the second.

Our contributions are:

\begin{enumerate}
\itemsep0em
\item \textbf{The phenomenon is real and general.} The benefit of align
fusion over concatenation changes \emph{sign} with the encoder, from
+0.87 AUROC to $-$1.68. All four effects survive a
Holm--Bonferroni correction over the 14 tests this paper reports
and all four are large relative to seed noise.
\item \textbf{Capacity is not what decides.} Two encoders from one family
differ by 3.42 AUROC under concatenation while their measured
alignment differs by about one point of recall. Their fusion benefits are
\emph{equivalent}, established by a two one-sided test against a margin fixed
before the numbers were seen rather than by a non-significant $p$-value.
\item \textbf{The usual explanation does not survive.} Over 20
encoder-language cells, measured alignment does not predict the fusion benefit
($r = -0.161$, $p = 0.499$). We close the two ways that null could be an
artefact: an attenuation correction bounds the true correlation at
$|r| \le 0.175$, and the 5 within-language fits are all
non-positive.
\item \textbf{The same dependence appears in the architecture.} Three
additions from \citet{memeclip2024} help on one encoder (+0.41,
$p = 0.015$) and hurt on another ($-$0.93,
$p = $<$0.001$), both significantly.
\end{enumerate}

No public Persian hateful-meme dataset exists and we report no Persian
classification number; what we offer instead is the measurement such a dataset
would be evaluated against.

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Fusion for hateful memes.} \citet{kiela2020hateful} introduced the
Hateful Memes Challenge with benign confounders that defeat unimodal models.
\citet{kumar2022hateclipper} freeze CLIP \citep{radford2021clip} and train a
shallow head over a feature interaction matrix, reporting that align fusion
beats concatenation. \citet{memeclip2024} keep the same fusion and add a
residual feature adapter, a semantically regularised loss and cosine
classifiers. \citet{rgcl2024} obtain stronger results with
retrieval-guided contrastive learning; we cite it as the stronger method and
make no claim of improving on it.

\textbf{What these share.} All three hold the encoder fixed and argue about
the fusion mechanism. If a property of the encoder decides how much fusion is
worth, then a result obtained on one encoder says little about another --- and
that is not testable with one encoder. This is the gap we address.

\textbf{Multilingual and low-resource settings.}
\citet{multi3hate2025} provide parallel memes in five languages with
per-country annotation, which lets a single head be read across languages
without confounding the content. \citet{crossmodal3600} provide
per-language captions for a shared image set, from which zero-shot retrieval
gives an alignment measure that no classifier training touches.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Fusion variants}

Given projected image and text features $p_i, p_t \in \mathbb{R}^n$:

\begin{align}
\textsc{concat} &= [\,p_i ; p_t\,] \in \mathbb{R}^{2n} \\
\textsc{align} &= p_i \odot p_t \in \mathbb{R}^{n} \\
\textsc{cross} &= \mathrm{vec}(p_i \otimes p_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{n^2}
\end{align}

\textsc{align} keeps the diagonal of the feature interaction matrix; the sum
of its elements is the dot product of the two vectors, so the vector itself is
a per-dimension view of how far the modalities agree. At $n = 1024$ the
\textsc{cross} variant places roughly a billion parameters in the first
classifier layer, which is why it is reported separately
(\S\ref{sec:limitations}).

\subsection{Alignment as a measured quantity}

The explanation under test names a property of the encoder's feature spaces,
so that property must be measured without the classifier. We use zero-shot
retrieval on Crossmodal-3600: given a caption, rank the images by cosine
similarity and ask whether the right one comes first. No labels and no
training are involved. On the 1{,}000-image slice we use, chance is
0.10\%, and every recall below should be read against it.

\subsection{Classifier head}

The encoders stay frozen, so the trainable part is one linear projection per
modality, the fusion, one pre-output layer with ReLU and dropout, and a linear
output. Frozen features depend on the encoder alone, so they are encoded once
and cached; this is what makes a sweep of this size affordable without
dedicated hardware.

\section{Experimental Setup}

\textbf{Encoders.} Four frozen encoders chosen to vary language coverage
rather than quality: CLIP ViT-L/14 and CLIP ViT-B/32, English-centred and
differing in capacity; jina-clip-v2, multilingual; and CLIPfa, a Persian
dual-tower model. CLIP and CLIPfa are mirror images --- each is strong in one
language and at chance in the other --- which is what makes the set a
controlled one.

\textbf{Protocol.} Every one of the nine hyperparameters of
\citet{kumar2022hateclipper} is held fixed across all cells. Each cell is
trained over 15 seeds. The checkpoint with the best validation AUROC on
\texttt{dev\_seen} is selected and \texttt{test\_seen} is evaluated once.

\textbf{Statistics.} All comparisons are paired over shared seeds and reported
with a paired $t$-test, Cohen's $d$ and a 95\% confidence interval. Claims
that two quantities do \emph{not} differ are made with two one-sided tests
(TOST) against a margin of 1.0 AUROC fixed before the numbers
were seen,
because a non-significant $p$-value is not evidence of equivalence. The
14 tests that carry \S\ref{sec:results} are corrected for
multiplicity with Holm--Bonferroni.

\subsection{The fusion benefit changes sign}

Table~\ref{tab:benefit} is the central result. Align fusion helps on both
CLIP variants, and \emph{hurts} on jina-clip-v2 and on CLIPfa. The effect
reported by \citet{kumar2022hateclipper} for one unseen language is therefore
neither confined to that language nor to a failure of the encoder: it reverses
on an encoder that is strong in the language being read.

Reported $p$-values are useful only up to the point where enough seeds make
any effect distinguishable from zero. We therefore give Cohen's $d$ beside
each: all four are large, meaning the effects are big relative to the
seed-to-seed noise, which more seeds do not change.

A tokeniser measurement gives the mechanism behind the gap. For captions of
the same images, CLIP spends 50.51 tokens on a Persian caption
against 12.60 on an English one, and its 77-token window --- an
architectural limit, not a setting --- truncates 11.4\% of the
Persian captions, where for jina-clip-v2 that figure is zero.

\subsection{Capacity is not what decides}

The explanation under test says alignment decides. The obvious rival says
capacity does. These are separable because CLIP ViT-L/14 and CLIP ViT-B/32
differ by 3.42 AUROC under concatenation --- a large gap in
Table~\ref{tab:main} --- while their measured alignment differs by about one
point of R@1.

Their fusion benefits are \textbf{equivalent}. The paired difference is
+0.25 with a 95\% interval of [$-$0.31, +0.81], and the two one-sided
tests reject at $p = 0.006$ against the pre-registered margin. An
effect of a
point or more is therefore \emph{excluded}, not merely unobserved --- and a
point is smaller than every fusion benefit this paper reports. We stress that
this is a different and stronger statement than a non-significant paired test,
which at an earlier seed count was all we had and excluded nothing.

\subsection{Architecture, the second axis}

The same dependence appears when the architecture is varied instead of the
fusion. The three additions of \citet{memeclip2024} help on CLIP ViT-L/14
(+0.41, $p = 0.015$) and hurt on jina-clip-v2
($-$0.93, $p = $<$0.001$). Both are significant; the sign flips
with the encoder.

\subsection{Correcting for multiplicity}

14 paired tests carry this section, so we correct them with
Holm--Bonferroni over a family fixed in advance. 12 of them hold.
The 2 that do not are exactly the two this paper reports as
\emph{null} --- the equivalence control above and one architecture cell ---
and a correction cannot weaken a claim that nothing differs, which is why the
TOST results are deliberately left uncorrected. The narrowest survivor is the
MemeCLIP effect on CLIP ViT-L/14, at $p = 0.0148$ against a
threshold of 0.0167; it is the claim a replication should be
expected to lose first, and we say so rather than leave a reader to find it.

\section{Testing the Prediction}

If the benefit is a property of alignment, it should be predictable from the
alignment of \emph{each} encoder-language pair, not only from four points on
one English corpus. A head trained on English Hateful Memes reads 300 parallel
memes zero-shot in five languages, over 5 seeds per cell, with each
cell's alignment taken from Crossmodal-3600 in that same language. Four
encoders over five languages is 20 points.

\textbf{It does not hold.} The correlation between alignment and fusion
benefit is $r = -0.161$ ($p = 0.499$), with Spearman
$\rho = -0.065$ ($p = 0.786$).

A negative result has two obvious explanations that have to be answered with
numbers rather than conceded.

\textbf{Measurement error.} Both variables are measured with error, which
attenuates any correlation toward zero. Between-cell spread is 2.12
against a typical within-cell standard error of 0.82, so the measure's
reliability is 0.85. Correcting for that attenuation still
bounds the true correlation at $|r| \le 0.175$. The null is not an
artefact of noise.

\textbf{Aggregation.} The 20-point axis compares languages, and
Crossmodal-3600's captions are written per language rather than translated, so
part of any cross-language gap is annotation style rather than encoder
ability. Fitting within each language is immune to that confound. All
5 within-language slopes are non-positive, from -0.63
to -0.02. Four points per language reach no significance
individually, but no language shows the predicted positive relationship.

So the phenomenon is confirmed and the explanation is refuted: the benefit
depends on the encoder, and the measured alignment is not what it depends on.

\section{Conclusion}

Whether cross-modal fusion is worth its cost depends on the encoder --- it
changes sign --- and not on the encoder's capacity. The explanation offered
for this in the literature, misaligned feature spaces, does not survive being
measured. For a practitioner working in a low-resource language the
consequence is concrete: the fusion must be ablated per encoder, because a
result obtained with another encoder does not transfer.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\textbf{Four encoders is four points.} The relationship in \S\ref{sec:results}
is read from four points and is not established by them. The paired and
interaction tests are valid over 15 shared seeds; the \emph{shape} of
the relationship is not.

\textbf{No Persian classification result.} No public Persian hateful-meme
dataset exists and this work had no annotation capacity to build one. The
Persian-facing claims here are measurements of encoders, not of Persian meme
classification, and they are not a substitute for it.

\textbf{CLIPfa operates near chance.} Its negative fusion benefit is measured
where the model barely works (62.60 AUROC against a chance
level of 50). The effect is stable across 15 seeds, so it is not
optimiser noise, but it remains an effect inside a weak regime.

\textbf{Cross fusion is absent from the ablation.} At the projection width
used here its first classifier layer would hold roughly a billion parameters.
The reference paper's own table shows cross fusion scoring \emph{below} align
while using some 380 times the parameters, so the missing cell is a missing
cost rather than a missing advantage.

\textbf{Absolute level.} Our concatenation row exceeds the configuration-
matched row of \citet{kumar2022hateclipper} while our align row falls below
it. The nine hyperparameters match, so the gap is not budget or optimiser; one
candidate we could not rule out is the width of the image features entering
the projection. Every claim here is a difference between two cells that read
one cache, in which such a choice largely cancels; the absolute level is what
moves.

\textbf{Single training corpus.} All classification training is on one
English corpus. The multilingual cells are zero-shot transfer, which is a
different and harder regime, and at 5 seeds rather than 15.
Those cells support a null, which correction moves upward, not a small
positive relationship, and none is claimed.

\section*{Ethics Statement}

This work studies the detection of hateful content and reports no model
intended for deployment. The Hateful Memes corpus is used under its licence
and is not redistributed. Multi3Hate is CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so no derived feature
cache leaves the machine it was computed on; reporting a measurement made from
those features is not distribution. jina-clip-v2 is CC BY-NC 4.0, which
permits this research use, and loading it executes code downloaded from its
model repository. A detector of hateful memes is dual-use: the same measure
that supports moderation supports evasion, and error rates differ across
languages in ways this paper measures rather than resolves.
